titel: Poggio on the trial of Jerome of Prague
autor: Poggio Bracciolini (1380–1459), Florentine humanist and papal secretary
quelle: F. Palacký (ed.), Documenta Mag. Joannis Hus vitam, doctrinam, causam in Constantiensi concilio actam ... illustrantia (Prague: Tempsky, 1869), no. 100, pp. 624–629. Internet Archive, documentamagjoa00palagoog. Public domain.
hinweis: Six excerpts covering most of the letter, read against the page images; cuts are marked [...]. The account of the burning is not carried. The English is this site's working translation (CC0); William Shepherd's English of 1802/1837 is in the public domain but too free to use here.

sections.titel: Poggio on the trial of Jerome of Prague
sections.blurb: A humanist at the council writes to Leonardo Bruni about the hearings of May 1416: Jerome's eloquence 'nearer to the ancients' than any he had heard, his wit, his roll of the unjustly condemned from Socrates to the apostles, his praise of Hus, and a man 'worthy of everlasting memory'.

units.titel: 'Nearer to the eloquence of the ancients'
units.orig: Poggius plurimam salutem dicit Leonardo Aretino. Cum pluribus diebus ad balnea fuissem, scripsi ad Nicolaum nostrum ex balneis ipsis epistolam, quam existimo te lecturum. Deinde, cum Constantiam revertissem, paucis post diebus coepta est agi causa Hieronymi, quem haereticum ferunt, et quidem publice. Hanc tibi recensere rationem institui, cum propter rei gravitatem, tum maxime propter eloquentiam hominis ac doctrinam. Fateor, me neminem unquam vidisse, qui in causa dicenda, praesertim capitis, magis accederet ad facundiam priscorum, quos tantopere admiramur. Mirum est vidisse, quibus verbis, qua facundia, quibus argumentis, quo vultu, quo ore, qua fiducia responderit adversariis, ac demum causam perorarit; ut dolendum sit, tam nobile ingenium, tamque excellens, ad illa haeresis studia divertisse, — prouti tamen vera sunt, quae sibi objiciuntur. Neque enim mei interest, tantam rem dijudicare: acquiesco eorum sententiis, qui sapientiores habentur.
units.en: Poggio sends Leonardo Aretino many greetings. When I had been at the baths for several days, I wrote from the baths themselves a letter to our Niccolò, which I think you will read. Then, when I had come back to Constance, a few days later the case of Jerome, whom they call a heretic, began to be heard, and in public. I have resolved to give you an account of it, both for the gravity of the matter and above all for the eloquence and learning of the man. I confess I never saw anyone who, in pleading a cause, above all a capital one, came nearer to the eloquence of the ancients whom we so admire. It was a wonder to see with what words, what fluency, what arguments, what countenance, what voice, what confidence he answered his adversaries and at last summed up his case; so that one must grieve that so noble and excellent a mind should have turned to those heretical studies, if indeed the charges brought against him are true. For it is not my business to judge so great a matter: I accept the opinions of those who are held to be wiser.
units.note: Poggio Bracciolini, the Florentine humanist, had come to Constance as a secretary of John XXIII and stayed after the pope's deposition. The letter to 'our Niccolò', Niccolò Niccoli, is his famous description of the baths at Baden. Leonardo Bruni of Arezzo ('Aretino'), his friend and fellow humanist, was in Florence. Note the clause 'if indeed the charges are true': it is the hinge of the letter, and Poggio at once withdraws from judging. Jerome had recanted before the council in September 1415; new charges were brought, and in May 1416 he was heard again.

units.orig: Cum multa in hunc Hieronymum congesta essent, quibus arguebatur haereticus, atque ea testibus firmata: tandem placuit, ut singulis, quae sibi objiciebantur, responderet. Ita in concionem deductus cum juberetur ad illa respondere, maledictis adversariorum diutius respondere recusavit, asserens, se prius causam suam agere, quam maledictis illorum respondere, itaque pro se prius dicentem se audiendum asserebat, tum ad aemulorum suorum probra in eum congesta deveniendum. Sed cum haec auditio sibi denegaretur, tum stans in medio concionis: „Quaenam est haec iniquitas! (inquit), ut cum CCCXL diebus, quibus in durissimis carceribus fui, in sordibus, in squalore, in stercore, in compedibus, in rerum omnium inopia, adversarios atque obtrectatores meos semper audieritis, me unam horam audire nolitis! Hinc est ut, cum singulorum aures patuerint atque in tam longo tempore vobis persuaserint, me haereticum, hostem fidei, ecclesiasticorum persecutorem, mihi autem defendendi nulla facultas detur, vos prius mentibus vestris me improbum hominem judicaveritis, quam, qui forem, potueritis cognoscere. Atqui, (inquit), homines estis, non dii, non perpetui, sed mortales, labi, errare, falli, decipi, seduci potestis. Hic mundi lumina, hic orbis terrarum prudentiores esse dicuntur: maxime vos decet elaborare, ne quid temere, ne quid inconsulte, aut quid praeter justitiam faciatis. Equidem ego homuncio sum, cujus de capite agitur; nec pro me loquor, qui mortalis: verum indignum videtur, sapientiam tot virorum adversum me aliquid statuere praeter aequitatem, non tantum re quantum exemplo nociturum.“ Haec et multa praeterea ornate disserebat in strepitu et murmure plurimorum sermonem ejus interpellantium.
units.en: Many things had been gathered against this Jerome by which he was charged as a heretic, and confirmed by witnesses; at last it was decided that he should answer each of the charges. So, brought before the assembly and ordered to answer them, he long refused to reply to his adversaries' slanders, saying that he should first plead his own cause and only then answer their abuse; he must be heard first speaking for himself, and then come to the insults his rivals had heaped on him. But when this hearing was denied him, standing in the midst of the assembly he said: 'What injustice is this, that for three hundred and forty days, which I have spent in the harshest prisons, in filth, in squalor, in dung, in fetters, in want of everything, you have always listened to my adversaries and slanderers, and will not listen to me for one hour! So it is that, while the ears of each of you have been open to them, and over so long a time they have persuaded you that I am a heretic, an enemy of the faith, a persecutor of churchmen, and I am given no means of defending myself, you have judged me a wicked man in your minds before you could know what I am. Yet you are men, not gods; not everlasting, but mortal; you can slip, err, be mistaken, deceived, led astray. Here, they say, are the lights of the world, the wisest men on earth: it most of all befits you to take care that you do nothing rashly, nothing thoughtlessly, nothing beyond justice. I am a little man whose head is at stake; nor do I speak for myself, who am mortal; but it seems unworthy that the wisdom of so many men should decree anything against me beyond equity, which will do harm not so much in the deed as in the example.' This and much more he set out with elegance, amid the noise and murmur of many interrupting him.
units.note: The first hearing was on 23 May 1416. The 'three hundred and forty days' are his own count of his imprisonment; he had been arrested in April 1415 and brought to Constance in chains.

units.orig: Tandem decretum est, ut ad errores, qui in eum conferebantur, publice responderet, deinde loquendi quae vellet facultas daretur. Legebantur ergo ex pulpito singula capita accusationis; tum rogabatur, an quid vellet objicere, et deinde testimoniis confirmabantur. Incredibile est dictu, quam callide responderet, quibus se tueretur argumentis. Nihil enim protulit indignum bono viro; et si id in fide sentiebat, quod verbis profitebatur, nulla in eum nedum mortis causa inveniri justa potuisset, sed nec quidem licuisset levissimae offensionis. Omnia falsa tunc esse dicebat, omnia crimina conficta ab aemulis suis. [...] Multos salibus perstrinxit, multos loedoriis; multos persaepe in re moesta ridere coëgit, jocando in illorum objurgationes. Cum rogaretur, quid sentiret de sacramento, inquit: „antea panem, in consecratione et postea verum corpus, et reliqua secundum fidem.“ Tum quidam: Atqui ajunt te dixisse, post consecrationem remanere panem. Respondit: „Apud pistorem remanet panis.“ Cuidam ex ordine Praedicatorum, acrius invehenti, „Tace (inquit) hypocrita!“ Alteri, conscientiam juranti: „Haec (inquit) tutissima via est ad fallendum.“ Quendam praecipuum adversarium numquam nisi canem aut asinum appellavit.
units.en: At last it was decreed that he should answer publicly to the errors charged against him, and then be given leave to say what he wished. So the articles of the accusation were read one by one from the pulpit; he was asked whether he wished to object, and then they were confirmed by testimony. It is beyond belief how skilfully he answered, with what arguments he defended himself. He said nothing unworthy of a good man; and if he believed in faith what he professed in words, no just cause could have been found against him, not of death, not even of the slightest offence. He said that everything was false, all the charges invented by his rivals. [...] He stung many with his wit, many with abuse; very often, in a sad business, he made many laugh, joking at their reproaches. When he was asked what he believed about the sacrament, he said: 'Before, bread; in the consecration and after, the true body; and the rest according to the faith.' Then someone said: 'But they say you said that after the consecration bread remains.' He answered: 'Bread remains at the baker's.' To a Dominican who inveighed against him too sharply he said: 'Be quiet, hypocrite!' To another, who swore by his conscience: 'That is the safest way to deceive.' One chief adversary he never called anything but a dog or an ass.
units.note: The Eucharist was the test the council applied to every Wycliffite: Wyclif had taught that the bread remains bread after consecration. Jerome's answer is orthodox and his joke turns the charge aside. Poggio's sentence 'if he believed in faith what he professed in words' is as close as he comes to an opinion. The cut is Jerome's protest that his enemies had made him out to be the enemy of all his judges.

units.orig: Data tandem, licet multis perstrepentibus, dicendi facultate, hic primum a deo exorsus est; eum deprecans rogabat, eam mentem sibi dari eamque dicendi facultatem, quae in commodum et salutem animae suae verteretur. Deinde: Scio, inquit, viri doctissimi, plures fuisse excellentes viros indigna suis virtutibus perpessos, falsis oppressos testibus, iniquis judiciis condemnatos. Incipiens autem a Socrate, illum injuste a suis damnatum esse retulit, neque cum posset evadere voluisse, ut duorum, quae hominibus asperrima videntur, metum demeret, carceris et mortis. [...] Postea ad Joannem baptistam, deinde ad salvatorem nostrum descendens, falsis testibus, falsis judiciis condemnatos inquit omnibus constare. Deinde Stephanum a sacerdotum collegio interfectum, apostolos autem omnes morte damnatos, non tamquam bonos, sed ut seditiosos populorum concitatores, contemtores deorum et malorum operum effectores. Iniquum esse, injuste damnari sacerdotem a sacerdote, at id factum esse docuit; iniquius a sacerdotum collegio, id quoque exemplo probavit; iniquissimum vero a concilio sacerdotum, id etiam accidisse monstravit. Haec diserte et magna cum exspectatione disseruit. [...] Addiderat enim, se sponte ad concilium venisse, ad se purgandum; vitam suam et studia exposuerat, officii plena et virtutis; dixerat, hunc morem priscis atque doctissimis viris fuisse, ut in rebus fidei invicem sententiis discreparent, non ad pessumdandum fidem, sed ad veritatem fidei aperiendam. Ita Augustinum et Hieronymum dissensisse asseruit, et non solum diversa sensisse, sed et contraria, nulla haereseos suspicione.
units.en: When at last, though many shouted, he was given leave to speak, he began with God, praying him to grant such a mind and such a power of speech as would turn to the profit and salvation of his soul. Then he said: 'I know, most learned men, that many excellent men have suffered what their virtues did not deserve, been crushed by false witnesses, condemned by unjust judgments.' Beginning with Socrates, he told how he was unjustly condemned by his own people, and would not escape when he could, to take away the fear of the two things that seem harshest to men, prison and death. [...] Then, coming down to John the Baptist and to our Saviour, he said all knew that they were condemned by false witnesses and false judgments. Then Stephen, killed by a college of priests, and all the apostles condemned to death, not as good men but as seditious stirrers of peoples, despisers of the gods and doers of evil works. It is unjust, he showed, for a priest to be condemned unjustly by a priest, and yet it had happened; more unjust by a college of priests, and he proved this too by example; most unjust of all by a council of priests, and he showed that this also had happened. All this he set out eloquently and with great expectation. [...] For he had added that he had come to the council of his own will, to clear himself; he had set out his life and studies, full of duty and virtue; he had said that it was the custom of the ancient and most learned men to differ in their opinions on matters of faith, not to destroy the faith but to bring its truth to light. So, he said, Augustine and Jerome had disagreed, and held not only different but contrary views, without any suspicion of heresy.
units.note: The second hearing, 26 May 1416. Poggio, a collector of classical manuscripts, hears a classical defence: the roll of the unjustly condemned runs from Socrates, Plato, Anaxagoras and Zeno (the first cut) through the prophets to Christ and the apostles. The climax, 'most unjust of all by a council of priests', was spoken to a council of priests. The second cut is Jerome's attack on the credibility of the witnesses, which, Poggio says, would have convinced in any case but one of faith.

units.orig: Exspectabant omnes, ut vel se purgaret, retractando objecta, vel erratorum veniam postularet. At ille, neque se errasse asseverans, neque se retractare aliorum falsa crimina velle ostendens, tandem descendit in laudationem Joannis Hus, dudum ad ignem damnati, virum illum bonum, justum et sanctum apellans et illa morte indignum; se quoque paratum quodvis supplicium subire forti animo atque constanti, seque inimicis suis cedere et testibus illis tam impudenter mentientibus, qui tamen aliquando coram deo, quem fallere non potuerint, essent rationem eorum quae dixissent reddituri. Magnus erat circumstantium dolor animi: cupiebant enim virum tam egregium salvari, si bona mens fuisset. Ille autem sua in sententia perseverans, ultro mortem appetere videbatur; laudansque Joannem Hus, ait, nihil illum adversus ecclesiae dei statum sensisse, sed adversus abusus clericorum, adversus superbiam, fastum ac pompam praelatorum. Nam cum patrimonia ecclesiarum primum deberentur pauperibus et advenis, ac demum fabricis, indignum illi bono viro videri, dispendi illa meretricibus, conviviis, equorum copiae aut canum saginae, cultui vestimentorum et aliis rebus indignis religione Christi.
units.en: Everyone expected that he would either clear himself by retracting what was charged, or ask pardon for his errors. But he, neither asserting that he had erred nor showing any wish to retract the false charges of others, at last came to the praise of Jan Hus, condemned to the fire some time before, calling him a good, just and holy man, unworthy of that death; he too, he said, was ready to undergo any punishment with a brave and steadfast mind, and yielded to his enemies and to those witnesses who lied so shamelessly, who would one day give account of what they had said before God, whom they could not deceive. Great was the grief of those standing round: for they wished so excellent a man to be saved, if his mind had been sound. But he, persisting in his view, seemed to seek death of his own accord; and praising Jan Hus, he said that Hus had held nothing against the state of the Church of God, but against the abuses of the clergy, against the pride, arrogance and pomp of prelates. For since the patrimonies of the churches were owed first to the poor and to strangers, and then to the fabric, it seemed unworthy to that good man that they should be squandered on harlots, banquets, troops of horses and the feeding of dogs, the adornment of clothes and other things unworthy of the religion of Christ.
units.note: This is the turn of the trial. Jerome had only to stand by his recantation of September 1415; instead he revoked it, and his praise of Hus made a second condemnation certain. His summary of Hus's teaching, against the abuses and not against the Church, is the reading of Hus that the Bohemian lords had given (Protest [1]); the Compare page sets the two side by side.

units.orig: Vox ejus suavis, aperta, resonans erat, quadam cum dignitate gestus oratoris, vel ad indignationem exprimendam, vel ad commovendam miserationem, quam tamen neque postulabat, neque consequi cupiebat. Stabat impavidus, intrepidus, mortem non contemnens solum, sed etiam appetens, ut alterum Catonem dixisses. O virum dignum memoria hominum sempiterna! Non laudo, si quid adversus instituta ecclesiae sentiebat; doctrinam admiror, rerum plurimarum scientiam, eloquentiam et argutiam respondendi: sed vereor, ne omnia in pestem suam sibi fuerint a natura concessa. Datum deinde spatium poenitendi biduo. Interim multi ad illum accessere viri eruditissimi, ut ipsum a sententia sua dimoverent. Inter quos cardinalis Florentinus eum adiit, ut ipsum flecteret ad rectam viam. Sed cum pertinacius in erroribus perseveraret, per concilium haereseos damnatus est et igni combustus. [...] Vidi hunc exitum, singulos actus inspexi: sive perfidia, sive pertinacia hoc egerit, certe ex philosophiae schola virum interemtum esse descripsisses. [...] Ex Constantia, III Kal. Junii, quo die Hieronymus poenas luit. Iterum vale, meque dilige.
units.en: His voice was sweet, clear and resonant, with an orator's dignity of gesture, whether to express indignation or to move pity, which he neither asked for nor wished to obtain. He stood unafraid, undaunted, not only despising death but seeking it, so that you would have called him another Cato. O man worthy of the everlasting memory of men! I do not praise him if he held anything against the institutions of the Church; I admire his learning, his knowledge of many things, his eloquence and his sharpness in reply; but I fear that all these were given him by nature for his own ruin. Then two days were given him to repent. Meanwhile many most learned men came to him to move him from his view, among them the cardinal of Florence, to bend him to the right way. But since he persisted all the more stubbornly in his errors, he was condemned by the council for heresy and burned. [...] I saw this end and watched each act: whether he did it from faithlessness or from stubbornness, you would certainly have described a man put to death out of the school of philosophy. [...] From Constance, on the third day before the Kalends of June, the day on which Jerome paid the penalty. Farewell again, and love me.
units.note: The cardinal of Florence was Francesco Zabarella, the canonist, who had argued that Jerome's recantation of 1415 should have ended the case. Jerome was condemned and burned on 30 May 1416, the day Poggio dated the letter. The first cut is Poggio's account of the execution, which this site does not reproduce; the second compares Jerome with Mucius Scaevola and with Socrates drinking the hemlock. Bruni answered by warning his friend to write more cautiously about such matters.
